title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles
book_title: The Triple-Levered Peninsula: Origins, Split Cycles, and Path Dependence

epigraph.quote: Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world—unless leverage and daily variance turn the exponent against you.
epigraph.author: Adapted from Quantitative Derivatives Practice

web_blocks.html: Direxion Daily MSCI South Korea Bull 3X ETF (KORU) (renamed from Shares in March 2026) is not a traditional operating company. It is a registered open-end management investment company operating as a series of the Direxion Shares ETF Trust (SEC CIK 0001424958, File No. 811-22201) [1][12]. The fund launched on April 10, 2013 and trades on NYSE Arca [1][6]. Rafferty Asset Management, LLC engineered KORU to seek daily investment results, before fees and expenses, equal to 300% (3X) of the daily performance of the MSCI Korea 25/50 Index [1][2][12]. The fund resets its derivative exposure at the close of each U.S. trading session [1]. Therefore, its corporate history does not center on factories or product launches [1]. Instead, it reflects South Korean equity cycles, Korean Won (KRW) currency swings, and mechanical share-count resets [1][2].

Over its thirteen-year lifespan, KORU's asset base and per-share net asset value (NAV) have experienced extreme cyclicality [1]. Unlike a 1x passive index tracker such as the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), a 3x daily leveraged fund amplifies both directional trends and intervening volatility [1]. KORU's NAV compounded rapidly during sustained bull runs in South Korean semiconductors and export cyclicals [1]. Key examples include the 2020–2021 global liquidity surge and the 2025 AI/High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) upcycle [1]. In contrast, the fund suffered severe capital erosion during protracted macro drawdowns [1]. In fiscal year 2022 (ended October 31, 2022), a global rate-tightening cycle collided with a memory-inventory glut [1]. KORU's audited NAV plunged -76.86% that year, dropping from a split-adjusted $261.20 to $60.00 per share [1]. Net assets contracted simultaneously to $20.09 million [1].

web_blocks.explanatory_p: Every major corporate action in KORU's history reflects mechanical share-price recalibration rather than fundamental value creation or destruction [3]. Key examples include its 1-for-10 reverse split in February 2025 and its 20-for-1 forward split in July 2026 [3].
web_blocks.takeaway: KORU's 13-year record proves it is a regime-dependent convexity engine: it compounds explosively in unidirectional uptrends (+231.64% in FY2025) and decays brutally in high-volatility drawdowns (-76.86% in FY2022) [1].

web_blocks.html: A critical turning point in KORU's modern cycle unfolded between February 2025 and November 2026 [1][3][8][9]. The fund first endured three consecutive years of lackluster or negative NAV performance from FY2022 through FY2024 [1]. Those drawdowns left its split-adjusted NAV hovering near $54.80–$55.70 [1]. In response, Direxion executed a 1-for-10 reverse split effective February 10, 2025, updating the CUSIP to 25461A387 [3]. Soon after, South Korean equities entered a powerful AI-memory and corporate-governance re-rating cycle [1]. By October 31, 2025, KORU's audited NAV surged +231.64% to $180.91, lifting net assets fourfold to $240.60 million [1]. Momentum continued into 1H FY2026: net assets reached $1,551.59 million by April 30, 2026 [8]. Direxion then executed a 20-for-1 forward split effective July 15, 2026 [3]. Following heavy creation-redemption swings, net assets stood at $1,256.39 million on July 31, 2026 and $747.35 million in November 2026 [6][9].

web_blocks.title: Path Dependence & The Split Illusion
paragraphs: Reverse and forward splits do not alter a shareholder's proportional ownership of fund net assets [3]. Even so, corporate splits serve as an essential forensic barometer for leveraged ETFs [3]. Frequent reverse splits indicate prolonged periods where realized volatility and downward drift eroded fund capital [3][5]. In contrast, a forward split signals an unusually sustained, unidirectional market advance [3].

web_blocks.html: To evaluate KORU's past cycles, an analyst must distinguish index-level return from currency-adjusted return [1][4]. The MSCI Korea 25/50 Index tracked by KORU is denominated in U.S. dollars [1][4]. The fund replicates that benchmark through U.S.-listed iShares MSCI South Korea ETF swaps [1]. As a result, every daily return embeds both local KOSPI equity moves and daily USD/KRW exchange-rate shifts [1][4]. During global risk-off shocks across emerging Asia, the Korean Won often depreciates against the U.S. dollar while Korean equities decline [4]. This dynamic creates a compounding double-negative daily impulse that KORU multiplies by three [1]. Conversely, when semiconductor exports surge and foreign capital enters Seoul, Won appreciation provides a secondary tailwind alongside 3x equity beta [4].

The sponsor's institutional pedigree also shapes how the vehicle behaves under market stress [1]. Rafferty Asset Management, LLC manages dozens of daily leveraged and inverse series within the Direxion Shares ETF Trust [1]. Unlike boutique single-product issuers, Direxion maintains standardized master ISDA swap agreements with Tier-1 global banks [1]. It also runs automated daily collateral-segregation workflows and enforces a contractual Operating Expense Limitation Agreement [1][2]. This infrastructure protects KORU against sponsor insolvency or single-day tracking failure [1]. Instead, the primary operational risk remains the unforgiving arithmetic of daily compounding over multi-month holding periods [5].

A simple two-day numerical illustration from the SEC's Investor Bulletin framework demonstrates why KORU's past cycles appear asymmetric [5]. Suppose the MSCI Korea 25/50 Index starts at 100, rises 10% on Day 1 to 110, and falls 9.09% on Day 2 back to 100 [5]. An unlevered holder finishes flat at 0.00% [5]. In comparison, a 3x daily fund starting at $100 gains 30% on Day 1 to $130 [5]. It then loses 27.27% (3 × 9.09%) on Day 2 to finish at $94.55 [5]. That leaves a -5.45% loss despite a flat underlying index [5]. Over 252 trading days in a volatile year like FY2022 or FY2023, thousands of micro-resets compound into severe divergence [1][5]. This compounding drag explains why KORU required a 1-for-10 reverse split in February 2025 before its AI-driven FY2025 rebound [1][3].

book_paragraphs: When you examine a traditional operating business, you start with a founder, a factory, or a piece of software. With KORU—officially renamed the Direxion Daily MSCI South Korea Bull 3X ETF in March 2026—you start with a mathematical contract wrapped in a 1940 Act fund. Launched on April 10, 2013 by Rafferty Asset Management under the Direxion Shares ETF Trust, KORU was never built to compound intrinsic value over decades. It was built to deliver three times the daily return of South Korea's equity market in a single, margin-free, NYSE Arca ticker.

To appreciate what that mandate means in practice, you only need to look at the fund's audited fiscal-year trail in the Direxion Shares ETF Trust Form N-CSR. Because KORU resets its leverage to 300% of net assets at the close of every single trading day, its multi-year history reads like a cardiogram of global semiconductor and emerging-market liquidity. In fiscal year 2021, riding the post-pandemic electronics and liquidity wave, KORU's net asset value rose 56.80%. Then came fiscal year 2022: global central banks tightened aggressively, memory-chip inventories piled up, and the Korean Won weakened. A unlevered investor in Korean stocks had a painful year; a 3x daily leveraged holder experienced a collapse. KORU's audited NAV fell 76.86% in a single fiscal year, shrinking from a split-adjusted $261.20 to $60.00, while total net assets contracted to just $20.09 million.

What followed in fiscal years 2023 and 2024 is even more instructive for you as a capital allocator. Even after the worst of the 2022 bear market ended, KORU did not smoothly snap back. In FY2023, the fund posted a -7.30% return, followed by a modest +4.21% in FY2024. Choppy, range-bound markets are the quiet enemy of daily leveraged funds because every up-day followed by a down-day forces the fund to buy high after gains and sell low after losses to maintain its 3x ratio. By early 2025, years of cumulative drag had compressed the nominal share price enough that Direxion filed a Form 497 supplement on January 10, 2025, executing a 1-for-10 reverse share split effective February 10, 2025, under a new CUSIP (25461A387).

And yet, just as reverse splits often mark the trough of a brutal cycle rather than the end of the story, South Korea's equity market was on the cusp of a violent regime shift. Driven by surging global demand for High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) chips used in artificial intelligence accelerators—a market dominated by South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics—alongside Seoul's Corporate Value-Up governance reforms, Korean equities entered a powerful, sustained uptrend. Because daily compounding works in your favor when daily returns cluster positively with low pullbacks, KORU's FY2025 audited NAV exploded higher by 231.64%, climbing from $55.70 to $180.91 per share as net assets quadrupled from $57.70 million to $240.60 million.

By April 30, 2026, that 1H FY2026 surge carried net assets from $240.60 million to $1.55 billion, prompting Direxion to execute a 20-for-1 forward split on July 15, 2026. Look closely at that seventeen-month round trip: a 1-for-10 reverse split in February 2025 followed by a 20-for-1 forward split in July 2026. After peaking near $1.55 billion in April and sitting at $1.26 billion on July 31, 2026, fund AUM moderated to $747.35 million by November 2026. Neither split created or destroyed a dollar of underlying economic value, yet together they capture KORU's core design: brutal erosion in choppy drawdowns and explosive convexity during persistent trends.

To see the mechanism behind that path dependence, walk through a simple two-day thought experiment with me. Imagine the MSCI Korea 25/50 Index starts at 100, surges 10% on Monday to 110, and drops 9.09% on Tuesday right back to 100. An unlevered investor in Seoul is completely flat. Now watch what happens to you in KORU starting at $100: on Monday you gain three times 10%, taking your stake to $130; on Tuesday you lose three times 9.09%, or 27.27%, knocking $130 down to $94.55. The underlying index went nowhere, yet you are down 5.45% in forty-eight hours.

Now multiply that two-day friction across 252 trading days in a choppy macro year, and add the Korean Won's habit of weakening against the U.S. dollar on the exact days global investors dump emerging-market risk. Because KORU's swaps reference the U.S.-dollar-denominated iShares MSCI South Korea ETF, equity selloffs and Won depreciation hit you simultaneously—and KORU multiplies both by three. Conversely, when foreign capital floods into Seoul during a memory-chip upcycle, Won strength and equity gains reinforce each other daily, turning that same compounding engine into a rocket booster. Understanding that symmetry—and asymmetry—is the first rule of touching this ticker.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The hardest mental adjustment when studying a 3x leveraged ETF is letting go of the idea that a ticker 'recovers' to its old highs. KORU's history—a -76.86% crash in FY2022, a 1-for-10 reverse split in early 2025, and a +231.64% surge in FY2025—teaches us that daily reset erases memory. You are never buying the 2013 or 2021 Korean market; you are buying today's 3x daily exposure to a semiconductor-heavy, Won-denominated index, and the path it takes over your exact holding window is everything.

section_takeaway: KORU is a 13-year-old, 3x daily leveraged ETF whose history of extreme drawdowns (-76.86% in FY2022), a 1-for-10 reverse split (Feb 2025), and explosive uptrend compounding (+231.64% in FY2025) demonstrates pure path-dependent convexity rather than traditional business compounding.
